title: 12 AM Notification
hook: Marketing wants to send a push notification to 10 million users at exactly 12:00 AM for the sale launch. Last time, the notification worked, and then your own servers went down.
context: Shopping app with 10M push-enabled users and a push provider with rate limits.
solution_brief: Batch and queue the audience, throttle to the provider's limit with backoff, isolate critical traffic in priority lanes, dedupe by deterministic ids, and stagger the blast so you do not DDoS yourself. Batches on a queue, progress per batch. Shared rate limiter, backoff with jitter on 429. Separate transactional and promotional lanes. Deterministic notification ids and collapse keys. Stagger sends and pre-warm for the response spike.

steps.prompt: A cron job loops over 10 million users and calls the push provider one by one from a single process. It would take hours, and a crash loses all progress. How do you restructure the send?
steps.context_note: The campaign must go out around midnight, and one process does all of it.

options.text: Split the audience into batches on a queue and let many workers process them, recording progress per batch.
Run the same loop on a faster machine.
Run the loop on three servers, each taking a third of the user list, with no shared record of progress.
Start the loop at 9 PM so it finishes by midnight.

steps.explanation: Batches on a queue turn one fragile long job into many small resumable ones, and throughput grows with the number of workers. After a crash only the unfinished batches are redone. Splitting the list across a few servers speeds it up but still loses progress when one fails, and starting early sends the sale announcement at the wrong time.
steps.bottleneck_note: Parallelise by splitting the audience, and make each unit of work resumable.

steps.prompt: 200 workers send as fast as they can, and the push provider starts returning HTTP 429 rate-limit errors. Each worker retries instantly in a loop, which makes things worse. What should the workers do?
steps.context_note: The provider caps how many pushes per second it accepts, however many workers you run.

options.text: Retry immediately until the provider accepts the request.
Share one limiter set to the provider's rate, back off with jitter on 429s, and let the queue hold the backlog.
Drop every notification that receives a 429.
Add more workers so more requests get through each second.

steps.explanation: The provider's limit is a hard external constraint, so total throughput has to stay under it. Backoff with jitter stops workers retrying in lockstep, and the queue absorbs what cannot be sent yet. Adding workers raises the request rate against a limit that is already being exceeded.
steps.bottleneck_note: Your slowest dependency sets your real throughput. Respect it with backpressure.

steps.prompt: During the blast, a user requests a login OTP push and another gets a payment alert, and both sit behind millions of promotional messages. How do you keep them from waiting?
steps.context_note: Promotional and critical messages share one sending path, so the OTP waits behind the whole backlog.

options.text: Keep one queue and process everything first-come, first-served.
Use separate queues for transactional and promotional messages, with sending capacity reserved for the critical one.
Send promotional messages more slowly for everyone, at all times.

steps.explanation: Separate lanes with reserved capacity stop bulk traffic from delaying time-sensitive messages. In a single first-come queue an OTP waits behind the whole promo backlog. Slowing every promotion permanently solves the problem for one night by hurting every future campaign.
steps.bottleneck_note: Isolate critical traffic from bulk traffic with separate queues and reserved capacity.

steps.prompt: A worker sent a batch and crashed before marking it done, so another worker re-sent it and users got the same promo twice. What reduces duplicate sends?
steps.context_note: The queue redelivers any batch whose worker died, and the provider may already have accepted it.

options.text: Give each (campaign, user) message a stable id, use the provider's dedupe key if it has one, and reconcile unclear attempts before retrying.
Mark each batch done before sending it, so it can never run twice.
Rely on the local sent ledger alone to skip users already marked as sent.
Lengthen the queue's visibility timeout so batches are never redelivered.

steps.explanation: A crash after the provider accepts a send but before your record is written leaves the outcome unknown, so a stable id and provider-side dedupe are the only way to suppress a repeat. Marking done first swaps duplicates for lost messages when a worker dies. A local ledger alone cannot see what the provider already did, and a longer timeout only delays redelivery.
steps.bottleneck_note: A local ledger cannot make an external send exactly once across a crash boundary.

steps.prompt: The push went out fine, but within seconds millions of people opened the app together and your own API fell over. What launch design prevents that?
steps.context_note: A push notification reaches every recipient at the same moment, and so does their reaction to it.

options.text: Send all 10 million at exactly 12:00:00 and autoscale the API when the traffic arrives.
Stagger the sends over 10 to 15 minutes, pre-warm the sale pages in a cache, and load test for the click burst.
Send to fewer users and hope that few of them open the app.

steps.explanation: Spreading the sends flattens the peak, and pre-warmed caches plus load testing make the remaining burst survivable. Autoscaling reacts over minutes, which is slower than a spike that arrives in seconds. Sending to fewer users shrinks the campaign instead of fixing the cause.
steps.bottleneck_note: Your notification system is a load generator pointed at your own backend.
